title: Some Basic Concepts of Chemistry
ref: NCERT Chemistry Part I · Unit 1 · pp. 1–28
note: Question text is taken from published copies of each paper (official NTA papers where available). Question numbers differ between booklet codes and shifts, so the exam, year and shift are shown instead. Every answer was worked out independently and compared with the published key.
multiRule: A question is listed under Multiple concepts when it needs two or more NCERT paragraphs. Plain mole conversion is used almost everywhere and does not count as a second concept on its own.

paragraphs.title: Gay Lussac's Law of Gaseous Volumes
Reactions in Solutions: Mass per cent

questions.q: The number of significant figures in 0.00340 is ____.
questions.sol: Leading zeros (0.00) only fix the decimal point and are not significant. The digits 3, 4 and the trailing 0 after the decimal point are significant: 3.
questions.hint: Zeros before the first non-zero digit don't count; trailing zeros after a decimal point do.

questions.q: Using the rules for significant figures, the correct answer for the expression (0.02858 × 0.112) / 0.5702 will be
questions.sol:
0.02858 × 0.112 ÷ 0.5702 = 0.0056138…

In multiplication/division the answer keeps as many significant figures as the least precise number: 0.112 has 3, so the answer is 0.00561.
questions.hint: Count significant figures in each number; the smallest count wins.

questions.q:
Which of the following have same number of significant figures?
A. 0.00253   B. 1.0003   C. 15.0   D. 163
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.sol:
0.00253 → 3 (leading zeros don't count); 1.0003 → 5 (zeros between digits count); 15.0 → 3 (trailing zero after the decimal counts); 163 → 3.

A, C and D each have 3.
questions.hint: Apply the zero rules one number at a time.

questions.q: Dalton's Atomic theory could not explain which of the following?
questions.sol:
Dalton's postulates (indivisible atoms, fixed whole-number ratios, atoms neither created nor destroyed) account for the three mass laws: conservation of mass, definite proportions and multiple proportions.

They cannot explain Gay-Lussac's law of gaseous volumes. Two volumes of H₂ and one volume of O₂ give two volumes of water vapour, which needs molecules that split into atoms. Avogadro later explained this; Dalton's model did not.
questions.hint: NCERT says it directly at the end of §1.5.

questions.check: Matches the published Code AA key
questions.q: In which case is the number of molecules of water maximum?
o: 0.00224 L of water vapours at 1 atm and 273 K
questions.sol:
Number of molecules ∝ number of moles, so convert each option to moles:

  • 0.00224 L ÷ 22.4 L mol⁻¹ = 10⁻⁴ mol
  • 0.18 g ÷ 18 g mol⁻¹ = 10⁻² mol
  • 18 mL of liquid water ≈ 18 g (density ≈ 1 g mL⁻¹) = 1 mol
  • 10⁻³ mol

18 mL of water holds 1 mol, i.e. NA molecules: the largest.
questions.hint: Turn every quantity into moles first.

questions.q: Which one of the followings has maximum number of atoms?
o: 1 g of O<sub>2</sub>(g) [Atomic mass of O = 16]
1 g of Li(s) [Atomic mass of Li = 7]
1 g of Ag(s) [Atomic mass of Ag = 108]
1 g of Mg(s) [Atomic mass of Mg = 24]
questions.sol:
Atoms = (mass ÷ molar mass) × atoms per formula unit × NA.

  • O₂: (1/32) × 2 = 1/16 NA
  • Li: 1/7 NA
  • Ag: 1/108 NA
  • Mg: 1/24 NA

For equal masses, the lightest atom gives the most atoms: lithium.
questions.hint: Equal masses → the smallest molar mass per atom wins. Don't forget O₂ is diatomic.

questions.q: The highest number of helium atoms is in
questions.sol:
• 4 mol → 4 NA atoms
  • 4 u is the mass of a single He atom → 1 atom
  • 4 g = 1 mol → NA atoms
  • At STP (273.15 K, 1 bar) one mole of gas occupies 22.7 L, so 2.271098 L = 0.1 mol → 0.1 NA atoms
questions.hint: u is the mass of one atom; g is the mass of one mole. At STP, 1 mol of gas = 22.7 L.

questions.q:
Among the following choose the ones with equal number of atoms.
A. 212 g of Na2CO3(s) [molar mass = 106 g]
B. 248 g of Na2O(s) [molar mass = 62 g]
C. 240 g of NaOH(s) [molar mass = 40 g]
D. 12 g of H2(g) [molar mass = 2 g]
E. 220 g of CO2(g) [molar mass = 44 g]
questions.sol:
Atoms = moles × atoms per formula unit (in units of NA):

  • A: 212/106 = 2 mol × 6 = 12
  • B: 248/62 = 4 mol × 3 = 12
  • C: 240/40 = 6 mol × 3 = 18
  • D: 12/2 = 6 mol × 2 = 12
  • E: 220/44 = 5 mol × 3 = 15

A, B and D each contain 12 NA atoms.
questions.hint: Count atoms per formula: Na₂CO₃ has 6, Na₂O 3, NaOH 3, H₂ 2, CO₂ 3.

questions.q:
The number of hydrogen atoms present in 5.4 g of urea is:
(Given: Molar mass of urea: 60 g mol−1, NA: 6.022 × 1023 particles mol−1)
questions.sol:
Urea is NH₂CONH₂: 4 H atoms per molecule.

n = 5.4 ÷ 60 = 0.09 mol → H atoms = 0.09 × 4 × 6.022 × 10²³ = 2.168 × 10²³.
questions.hint: Moles of urea × 4 × N<sub>A</sub>.
questions.trap: Using 2 H per molecule gives 1.084 × 10²³, which is one of the options.

questions.q: The number of chlorine atoms in 20 mL of chlorine gas at STP is ____ × 10<sup>21</sup>. (Round off to the Nearest Integer) [Assume chlorine is an ideal gas at STP; R = 0.083 L bar mol<sup>−1</sup> K<sup>−1</sup>, N<sub>A</sub> = 6.023 × 10<sup>23</sup>]
questions.hint: Moles of Cl₂ first; then remember each molecule has 2 atoms.

questions.q: The number of N atoms in 681 g of C<sub>7</sub>H<sub>5</sub>N<sub>3</sub>O<sub>6</sub> is x × 10<sup>21</sup>. The value of x is ____. (N<sub>A</sub> = 6.02 × 10<sup>23</sup> mol<sup>−1</sup>) (Nearest Integer)
questions.hint: Moles of compound × atoms of N per molecule × N<sub>A</sub>.

questions.q: The number of molecules and moles in 2.8375 litres of O<sub>2</sub> at STP are respectively
questions.hint: At STP (1 bar), 1 mol of gas = 22.7 L.

questions.q: Find percentage nitrogen by mass in Histamine?
questions.sol:
Histamine is C₅H₉N₃ (an imidazole ring with a –CH₂CH₂NH₂ side chain): molar mass = 5(12) + 9(1) + 3(14) = 111 g mol⁻¹.

% N = 42 ÷ 111 × 100 = 37.84%.
questions.hint: Write the molecular formula first, then mass of N ÷ molar mass × 100.
questions.trap: You need histamine's formula (C₅H₉N₃); the arithmetic is the easy part.

questions.q: Hemoglobin contains 0.34% of iron by mass. The number of Fe atoms in 3.3 g of hemoglobin is: (Given: Atomic mass of Fe is 56 u, N<sub>A</sub> is 6.022 × 10<sup>23</sup> mol<sup>−1</sup>)
questions.hint: Mass of Fe from the percentage, then moles × N<sub>A</sub>.

questions.check: NTA final answer key (Code P3): option 4
questions.q: An organic compound contains 78% (by wt.) carbon and remaining percentage of hydrogen. The right option for the empirical formula of this compound is: [Atomic wt. of C is 12, H is 1]
questions.sol:
Take 100 g: C = 78 g → 78/12 = 6.5 mol; H = 22 g → 22 mol.

Divide by the smaller: C : H = 1 : 3.38. Of the options, CH₃ (1 : 3) is the closest, and NTA's final key gives CH₃.

Note: the data do not give a clean whole-number ratio. CH₃ would need 80% carbon exactly (12/15). Pick the nearest option in the exam.
questions.hint: Assume 100 g, convert % to moles, divide by the smallest.

questions.q:
A compound X contains 32% of A, 20% of B and remaining percentage of C. Then, the empirical formula of X is:
(Given atomic masses of A = 64; B = 40; C = 32 u)
questions.sol:
C = 100 − 32 − 20 = 48%.

  • A: 32/64 = 0.5
  • B: 20/40 = 0.5
  • C: 48/32 = 1.5

Divide by 0.5 → 1 : 1 : 3, so the empirical formula is ABC₃.
questions.hint: Find % of C first, then mole ratio.

questions.q: Number of hydrogen atoms per molecule of a hydrocarbon A having 85.8% carbon is ____. (Given: Molar mass of A = 84 g mol<sup>−1</sup>)
questions.hint: Mass of C per molecule = % × molar mass.

questions.q: A metal chloride contains 55.0% of chlorine by weight. 100 mL vapours of the metal chloride at STP weigh 0.57 g. The molecular formula of the metal chloride is (Given: Atomic mass of chlorine is 35.5 u)
questions.sol:
Molar mass = 0.57 g × (22700 mL ÷ 100 mL) = 129.4 g mol⁻¹.

Cl per molecule = 0.55 × 129.4 = 71.2 g = 2 Cl → MCl₂.
questions.hint: Vapour mass at STP gives the molar mass.

questions.q: If a compound contains 54.2% carbon, 9.2% hydrogen and the rest is oxygen. What is molecular formula of the compound, if molecular mass is 132 g/mol?
questions.hint: Empirical formula first, then n = molar mass ÷ empirical formula mass.

questions.q: A compound contains 14.4% carbon, 1.2% hydrogen and 84.4% chlorine, calculate empirical formula mass of compound. [Molar mass of C = 12, H = 1, Cl = 35.5]
questions.sol:
Moles: C 1.2, H 1.2, Cl 2.38 → ratio 1 : 1 : 2 → CHCl₂.

Empirical formula mass = 12 + 1 + 71 = 84.
questions.hint: Divide each % by its atomic mass, then by the smallest.

questions.check: Matches the published Code AA key
questions.q: A mixture of 2.3 g formic acid and 4.5 g oxalic acid is treated with conc. H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>. The evolved gaseous mixture is passed through KOH pellets. Weight (in g) of the remaining product at STP will be
questions.sol:
Conc. H₂SO₄ removes water from both acids:

  • HCOOH → CO + H₂O: 2.3/46 = 0.05 mol → 0.05 mol CO
  • H₂C₂O₄ → CO + CO₂ + H₂O: 4.5/90 = 0.05 mol → 0.05 mol CO + 0.05 mol CO₂

KOH absorbs the CO₂. What remains is CO: 0.10 mol × 28 g mol⁻¹ = 2.8 g.
questions.hint: Write both decomposition equations; KOH removes only the acidic gas (CO₂).

questions.q: The number of moles of hydrogen molecules required to produce 20 moles of ammonia through Haber's process is:
questions.sol:
N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) → 2NH₃(g). Mole ratio H₂ : NH₃ = 3 : 2.

H₂ needed = 20 × 3/2 = 30 mol.
questions.hint: Read the mole ratio straight off the balanced equation.

questions.q: When 1 dm<sup>3</sup> of CO<sub>2</sub> gas is passed over hot coke, the volume of gaseous mixture after complete reaction at STP becomes 1.4 dm<sup>3</sup>. The composition of the gaseous mixture at STP is:
o: 0.6 dm<sup>3</sup> of CO, 0.8 dm<sup>3</sup> of CO<sub>2</sub>
0.8 dm<sup>3</sup> of CO, 0.8 dm<sup>3</sup> of CO<sub>2</sub>
0.6 dm<sup>3</sup> of CO, 0.4 dm<sup>3</sup> of CO<sub>2</sub>
0.8 dm<sup>3</sup> of CO, 0.6 dm<sup>3</sup> of CO<sub>2</sub>
questions.sol:
CO₂(g) + C(s) → 2CO(g). At the same T and p, gas volumes are in the same ratio as moles.

If x dm³ of CO₂ reacts, it makes 2x dm³ of CO: total = (1 − x) + 2x = 1 + x = 1.4 → x = 0.4.

CO = 0.8 dm³, CO₂ left = 0.6 dm³.
questions.hint: Coke is a solid, so only CO₂ and CO count towards the gas volume.

questions.q: 5 g of Zn reacts with (I) Excess of NaOH (II) Dilute HCl, then volume ratio of H<sub>2</sub> gas evolved in (I) and (II) is
questions.sol:
Zn + 2NaOH → Na₂ZnO₂ + H₂ and Zn + 2HCl → ZnCl₂ + H₂.

In both, 1 mol Zn gives 1 mol H₂, so the same 5 g of Zn gives the same volume of H₂: ratio 1 : 1.
questions.hint: Write both balanced equations and compare mol H₂ per mol Zn.

questions.q: The minimum number of moles of O<sub>2</sub> required for complete combustion of 1 mole of propane and 2 moles of butane is ____.
questions.sol:
C₃H₈ + 5O₂ → 3CO₂ + 4H₂O: 1 mol propane needs 5 mol O₂.

C₄H₁₀ + 13/2 O₂ → 4CO₂ + 5H₂O: 2 mol butane need 13 mol O₂.

Total = 18 mol.
questions.hint: O₂ for CₓHᵧ = x + y/4 per mole.

questions.q: Complete combustion of 3 g of ethane gives x × 10<sup>22</sup> molecules of water. The value of x is ____. (Round off to the Nearest Integer) [Use: N<sub>A</sub> = 6.023 × 10<sup>23</sup>; Atomic masses in u: C: 12.0; O: 16.0; H: 1.0]
questions.sol:
3 g C₂H₆ = 0.1 mol. Each C₂H₆ gives 3 H₂O, so 0.3 mol H₂O.

Molecules = 0.3 × 6.023 × 10²³ = 18.07 × 10²² → 18.
questions.hint: Count H: 6 H in ethane → 3 H₂O.

questions.q: C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>COOH + Br<sub>2</sub> —FeBr<sub>3</sub>→ m-BrC<sub>6</sub>H<sub>4</sub>COOH + HBr. Consider the above reaction where 6.1 g of benzoic acid is used to get 7.8 g of m-bromo benzoic acid. The percentage yield of the product is ____. (Round off to the Nearest integer) [Given: Atomic masses: C = 12.0 u, H: 1.0 u, O: 16.0 u, Br = 80.0 u]
questions.sol:
6.1 g benzoic acid (122 g mol⁻¹) = 0.05 mol → theoretical 0.05 mol m-bromobenzoic acid (201 g mol⁻¹) = 10.05 g.

% yield = 7.8 ÷ 10.05 × 100 = 77.6 ≈ 78.
questions.hint: Theoretical yield from the 1 : 1 mole ratio, then actual ÷ theoretical.

questions.q: The moles of methane required to produce 81 g of water after complete combustion is ____ × 10<sup>−2</sup> mol. [nearest integer]
questions.sol: CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O. 81 g H₂O = 4.5 mol, so CH₄ = 4.5 ÷ 2 = 2.25 mol = 225 × 10⁻² mol.
questions.hint: 1 mol CH₄ gives 2 mol H₂O.

questions.q: SO<sub>2</sub>Cl<sub>2</sub> on reaction with excess of water results into acidic mixture: SO<sub>2</sub>Cl<sub>2</sub> + 2H<sub>2</sub>O → H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> + 2HCl. 16 moles of NaOH is required for the complete neutralisation of the resultant acidic mixture. The number of moles of SO<sub>2</sub>Cl<sub>2</sub> used is:
questions.sol:
1 mol SO₂Cl₂ gives 1 mol H₂SO₄ (2 H⁺) + 2 mol HCl (2 H⁺) = 4 mol H⁺, which needs 4 mol NaOH.

16 mol NaOH ÷ 4 = 4 mol SO₂Cl₂.
questions.hint: Count acidic H⁺ produced per SO₂Cl₂.

questions.q: 56.0 L of nitrogen gas is mixed with excess of hydrogen gas and it is found that 20 L of ammonia gas is produced. The volume of unused nitrogen gas is found to be ____ L.
questions.sol:
N₂ + 3H₂ → 2NH₃. At the same conditions volumes are in the mole ratio, so 20 L NH₃ used 10 L N₂.

Unused N₂ = 56.0 − 10 = 46 L.
questions.hint: Gas volumes follow the coefficients (1 N₂ : 2 NH₃).

questions.q: The volume of hydrogen liberated at STP by treating 11.5 g of zinc with excess HCl is ____ L. (Nearest integer) (Given: Molar mass of Zn is 65.4 g mol<sup>−1</sup> and Molar volume of H<sub>2</sub> at STP = 22.7 L)
questions.hint: 1 mol Zn → 1 mol H₂; use 22.7 L per mole at STP.

questions.q: Moles of CH<sub>4</sub> required for formation of 22 g of CO<sub>2</sub> is m × 10<sup>−2</sup>. The value of m is:
questions.sol: CH₄ → CO₂ (1 : 1). 22 g CO₂ = 0.5 mol, so CH₄ = 0.5 mol = 50 × 10⁻².
questions.hint: One carbon in, one carbon out.

questions.q: CNG is an important transportation fuel. When 100 g CNG is mixed with 208 g oxygen in vehicles, it leads to the formation of CO<sub>2</sub> and H<sub>2</sub>O and produces large quantity of heat during this combustion, then the amount of carbon dioxide, produced in grams is ____. [nearest integer] [Assume CNG to be methane]
questions.sol:
CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O. CH₄ = 100 ÷ 16 = 6.25 mol; O₂ = 208 ÷ 32 = 6.5 mol, enough for only 3.25 mol CH₄, so O₂ is limiting.

CO₂ = 3.25 mol × 44 = 143 g.
questions.hint: Divide each reactant's moles by its coefficient; the smaller one limits.

questions.q: Production of iron in blast furnace follows the following equation: Fe<sub>3</sub>O<sub>4</sub>(s) + 4CO(g) → 3Fe(l) + 4CO<sub>2</sub>(g). When 4.640 kg of Fe<sub>3</sub>O<sub>4</sub> and 2.520 kg of CO are allowed to react then the amount of iron (in g) produced is: [Given: Molar atomic mass (g mol<sup>−1</sup>): O = 16, Fe = 56, C = 12]
questions.sol:
Fe₃O₄ = 4640 ÷ 232 = 20 mol (needs 80 mol CO); CO = 2520 ÷ 28 = 90 mol. Fe₃O₄ is limiting.

Fe = 3 × 20 = 60 mol × 56 = 3360 g.
questions.hint: Compare moles available with the 1 : 4 ratio.

questions.q: In the given reaction, X + Y + 3Z ⇌ XYZ<sub>3</sub>, if one mole of each of X and Y with 0.05 mol of Z gives compound XYZ<sub>3</sub>. (Given: Atomic masses of X, Y and Z are 10, 20 and 30 amu, respectively.) The yield of XYZ<sub>3</sub> is ____ g. (Nearest integer)
questions.sol:
Z is needed 3 per formula unit: 0.05 mol Z makes only 0.05 ÷ 3 = 0.0167 mol XYZ₃, so Z is limiting.

Molar mass XYZ₃ = 10 + 20 + 90 = 120 g mol⁻¹ → 0.0167 × 120 = 2 g.
questions.hint: Z has coefficient 3, so divide its moles by 3.

questions.q: N<sub>2</sub>(g) + 3H<sub>2</sub>(g) ⇌ 2NH<sub>3</sub>(g), with 20 g of N<sub>2</sub> and 5 g of H<sub>2</sub>. Consider the above reaction, the limiting reagent of the reaction and number of moles of NH<sub>3</sub> formed respectively are:
questions.sol:
N₂ = 20 ÷ 28 = 0.714 mol (needs 2.14 mol H₂); H₂ = 2.5 mol. N₂ is limiting.

NH₃ = 2 × 0.714 = 1.42 mol.
questions.hint: mol ÷ coefficient: N₂ 0.71, H₂ 0.83.

questions.q: When 12 g carbon is burnt in 48 g of oxygen, the volume of carbon monoxide produced is ____ × 10<sup>−1</sup> L at STP [nearest integer]. [Given: Assume CO as ideal gas, Mass of C is 12 g mol<sup>−1</sup>, Mass of O is 16 g mol<sup>−1</sup> and molar volume of an ideal gas at STP is 22.7 L mol<sup>−1</sup>]
questions.sol:
2C + O₂ → 2CO. C = 1 mol, O₂ = 1.5 mol (needs only 0.5 mol), so carbon is limiting.

CO = 1 mol = 22.7 L = 227 × 10⁻¹ L.
questions.hint: The question fixes the product as CO; just find the limiting reagent.

questions.q: 2.32 × 10<sup>3</sup> kg of Fe<sub>3</sub>O<sub>4</sub> reacts with 2.8 × 10<sup>3</sup> kg of CO according to the following reaction: Fe<sub>3</sub>O<sub>4</sub> + CO → CO<sub>2</sub> + Fe. If x kg of Fe is formed. Find the value of x?
questions.sol:
Balanced: Fe₃O₄ + 4CO → 3Fe + 4CO₂. Fe₃O₄ = 2.32 × 10⁶ g ÷ 232 = 10⁴ mol (needs 4 × 10⁴ mol CO); CO = 10⁵ mol, in excess.

Fe = 3 × 10⁴ mol × 56 g = 1.68 × 10⁶ g = 1680 kg.
questions.hint: Balance the equation first.

questions.check: Worked out independently (the source copy prints no answer key)
questions.q:
A + 2B → AB2. 36.0 g of 'A' (Molar mass: 60 g mol−1) and 56.0 g of 'B' (Molar mass: 80 g mol−1) are allowed to react. Which of the following statements are correct?
A. 'A' is the limiting reagent.
B. 77.0 g of AB2 is formed.
C. Molar mass of AB2 is 140 g mol−1.
D. 15.0 g of A is left unreacted after the completion of reaction.
questions.sol:
A = 0.6 mol, B = 0.7 mol (needs 1.2 mol for all of A), so B is limiting: statement A is false.

AB₂ = 0.35 mol; molar mass = 60 + 2 × 80 = 220 (C false) → 77.0 g (B true). A left = 0.6 − 0.35 = 0.25 mol = 15.0 g (D true). Answer: B and D only.
questions.hint: Divide moles by coefficients to find the limiting reagent.

questions.q: C is added to a solution of A and B. The mole fraction of C is:
questions.sol: Mole fraction = moles of that component ÷ total moles of all components: xC = nC / (nA + nB + nC).
questions.hint: The denominator is the total number of moles.

questions.check: Matches the published Code A key
questions.q: Which of the following is dependent on temperature?
questions.sol:
Molarity = moles per litre of solution. Volume expands or contracts with temperature, so molarity changes.

Molality, mole fraction and mass % use only masses or mole counts, which do not change with temperature.
questions.hint: Which term has a volume in it?

questions.q: When 800 mL of 0.5 M nitric acid is heated in a beaker, its volume is reduced to half and 11.5 g of nitric acid is evaporated. The molarity of the remaining nitric acid solution is x × 10<sup>−2</sup> M. (Nearest Integer) (Molar mass of nitric acid is 63 g mol<sup>−1</sup>)
questions.sol:
Initial HNO₃ = 0.8 × 0.5 = 0.40 mol; lost 11.5 ÷ 63 = 0.183 mol; left 0.217 mol in 0.400 L.

Molarity = 0.544 M = 54 × 10⁻² M.
questions.hint: Track moles of HNO₃, then divide by the new volume.

questions.q: The quantity which changes with temperature is:
questions.sol: Molarity uses the volume of solution, which expands or contracts with temperature. The other three depend only on masses or moles.
questions.hint: Look for a volume in the definition.

questions.q: 200 mL of 0.2 M solution of NaOH is mixed with 400 mL of 0.5 M NaOH solution. Molarity of mixture is
questions.hint: Add the moles, add the volumes.

questions.q: In one molal solution that contains 0.5 mole of a solute, there is
questions.sol: Molality = moles of solute ÷ kg of solvent → 1 = 0.5 ÷ W, so W = 0.5 kg = 500 g of solvent.
questions.hint: Molality is per kg of solvent, a mass, not a volume.
questions.trap: 500 mL looks tempting, but molality never uses volume.

questions.q:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled as Assertion (A) and the other is labelled as Reason (R).
Assertion (A): At 10°C, the density of a 5M solution of KCl [atomic masses of K and Cl are 39 & 35.5 g mol−1]. The solution is cooled to −21°C. The molality of the solution will remain unchanged.
Reason (R): The molality of a solution does not change with temperature as mass remains unaffected with temperature.
In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:
o: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)
Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A)
questions.sol: Molality is moles of solute per kg of solvent. Cooling changes volumes but not masses, so molality stays the same. The reason states exactly why the assertion holds: both true, R explains A.
questions.hint: Which concentration terms use only masses?

questions.q: The number of atoms in a silver plate having area 0.05 cm<sup>2</sup> and thickness 0.05 cm is ____ × 10<sup>19</sup>. Density of silver is 7.9 g/cm<sup>3</sup>.
questions.hint: Volume → mass (density) → moles → atoms.

questions.q: The molality of a 10% (v/v) solution of di-bromine solution in CCl<sub>4</sub> (carbon tetrachloride) is 'x'. x = ____ × 10<sup>−2</sup> M. (Nearest integer) [Given: molar mass of Br<sub>2</sub> = 160 g mol<sup>−1</sup>, atomic mass of C = 12 g mol<sup>−1</sup>, atomic mass of Cl = 35.5 g mol<sup>−1</sup>, density of dibromine = 3.2 g cm<sup>−3</sup>, density of CCl<sub>4</sub> = 1.6 g cm<sup>−3</sup>]
questions.sol:
100 mL solution: 10 mL Br₂ (32 g = 0.2 mol) and 90 mL CCl₄ (144 g = 0.144 kg).

Molality = 0.2 ÷ 0.144 = 1.39 m → 139.
questions.hint: Convert each volume to mass with its density.

questions.check: Worked out independently (the source copy prints no answer key)
questions.q: 80 mL of a hydrocarbon on mixing with 264 mL of oxygen in a closed U-tube undergoes complete combustion. The residual gases after cooling to 273 K occupy 224 mL. When the system is treated with KOH solution, the volume decreases to 64 mL. The formula of the hydrocarbon is:
questions.sol:
KOH absorbs CO₂: CO₂ = 224 − 64 = 160 mL; leftover O₂ = 64 mL, so O₂ used = 200 mL.

CₓHᵧ + (x + y/4)O₂ → xCO₂: 80x = 160 → x = 2; 80(x + y/4) = 200 → y = 2. Hydrocarbon = C₂H₂.
questions.hint: Gas volumes behave like moles (Gay Lussac); KOH removes only CO₂.

questions.q: 6.023 × 10<sup>22</sup> molecules are present in 10 g of a substance 'x'. The molarity of a solution containing 5 g of substance 'x' in 2 L solution is ____ × 10<sup>−3</sup>.
questions.sol:
6.023 × 10²² molecules = 0.1 mol, so 10 g is 0.1 mol and the molar mass is 100 g mol⁻¹.

5 g = 0.05 mol in 2 L → 0.025 M = 25 × 10⁻³ M.
questions.hint: Number of molecules → moles → molar mass.

questions.q:
The right option for the mass of CO2 produced by heating 20 g of 20% pure limestone is (Atomic mass of Ca = 40)
[CaCO3 —1200 K→ CaO + CO2]
questions.sol:
Only the pure part reacts: 20% of 20 g = 4 g CaCO₃ = 4/100 = 0.04 mol.

1 mol CaCO₃ → 1 mol CO₂, so CO₂ = 0.04 × 44 = 1.76 g.
questions.hint: Apply the purity first, then the 1 : 1 mole ratio.
questions.trap: Treating all 20 g as CaCO₃ gives 8.8 g of CO₂, which is five times too much. The impurity does not release CO₂.

questions.q:
What mass of 95% pure CaCO3 will be required to neutralise 50 mL of 0.5 M HCl solution according to the following reaction?
CaCO3(s) + 2HCl(aq) → CaCl2(aq) + CO2(g) + H2O(l)
[Calculate upto second place of decimal point]
questions.hint: Molarity × volume → moles of HCl → halve → mass → divide by purity.
questions.trap: 1.25 g is the pure mass; forgetting the 95% purity gives that option.

questions.q: The ratio of the mass percentages of 'C & H' and 'C & O' of a saturated acyclic organic compound 'X' are 4 : 1 and 3 : 4 respectively. Then, the moles of oxygen gas required for complete combustion of two moles of organic compound 'X' is ____.
questions.sol:
Mass ratio C : H : O = 12 : 3 : 16 (C : H = 4 : 1 and C : O = 3 : 4). Mole ratio = 1 : 3 : 1, so the empirical formula is CH₃O.

A saturated acyclic compound with this ratio is C₂H₆O₂ (ethylene glycol).

2C₂H₆O₂ + 5O₂ → 4CO₂ + 6H₂O, so 2 mol X needs 5 mol O₂.
questions.hint: Mass ratios → mole ratio → empirical formula → a real saturated molecule → balance combustion.

questions.q: A reaction of 0.1 mole of Benzylamine with bromomethane gave 23 g of Benzyl trimethyl ammonium bromide. The number of moles of bromomethane consumed in this reaction are n × 10<sup>−1</sup>, when n = ____. (Round off to the Nearest Integer) (Given: Atomic masses: C: 12.0 u, H: 1.0 u, N: 14.0 u, Br: 80.0 u)
questions.sol:
C₆H₅CH₂NH₂ + 3CH₃Br → C₆H₅CH₂N(CH₃)₃⁺Br⁻ + 2HBr: three methyl groups end up on N.

Product C₁₀H₁₆NBr = 230 g mol⁻¹, so 23 g = 0.1 mol, which needs 0.3 mol CH₃Br → n = 3.
questions.hint: How many CH₃ groups does the quaternary salt carry?

questions.q: 28.0 L of CO<sub>2</sub> is produced on complete combustion of 16.8 L gaseous mixture of ethene and methane at 25 °C and 1 atm. Heat evolved during the combustion process is ____ kJ. Given: ΔH<sub>c</sub>(CH<sub>4</sub>) = −900 kJ mol<sup>−1</sup>, ΔH<sub>c</sub>(C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>4</sub>) = −1400 kJ mol<sup>−1</sup>
questions.sol:
Let ethene = x L: it gives 2x L CO₂, methane gives (16.8 − x) L. 2x + 16.8 − x = 28.0 → x = 11.2 L ethene, 5.6 L methane.

At 25 °C and 1 atm, 1 mol = 24.4 L: ethene 0.458 mol, methane 0.229 mol.

Heat = 0.458 × 1400 + 0.229 × 900 = 641 + 206 = 847 kJ.
questions.hint: Use the CO₂ volume to split the mixture, then convert volumes to moles.

questions.check: Worked out independently (the source copy prints no answer key)
questions.q: 14.0 g of calcium metal is allowed to react with excess HCl at 1.0 atm pressure and 273 K. Which of the following statements is incorrect? [Given: Molar mass in g mol<sup>−1</sup> of Ca − 40, Cl − 35.5, H − 1]
o: 7.84 L of H<sub>2</sub> gas is evolved.
The limiting reagent is calcium metal.
0.35 mol of H<sub>2</sub> gas is evolved.
questions.sol:
Ca + 2HCl → CaCl₂ + H₂. 14.0 g Ca = 0.35 mol (HCl in excess, so Ca limits).

H₂ = 0.35 mol = 0.35 × 22.4 L (1 atm, 273 K) = 7.84 L ✓. CaCl₂ = 0.35 × 111 = 38.9 g, not 33.3 g, so (A) is incorrect.
questions.hint: Check each statement from 0.35 mol Ca.

questions.q: Consider titration of NaOH solution versus 1.25 M oxalic acid solution. At the end point following burette readings were obtained: (i) 4.5 mL (ii) 4.5 mL (iii) 4.4 mL (iv) 4.4 mL (v) 4.4 mL. If the volume of oxalic acid taken was 10.0 mL then the molarity of the NaOH solution is ____ M. (Rounded-off to the nearest integer)
questions.sol:
Use the concordant reading, 4.4 mL (it appears three times).

H₂C₂O₄ + 2NaOH → Na₂C₂O₄ + 2H₂O. Oxalic acid = 1.25 × 10.0 = 12.5 mmol, so NaOH = 25 mmol.

M(NaOH) = 25 ÷ 4.4 = 5.7 ≈ 6 M.
questions.hint: Pick the concordant reading; oxalic acid is dibasic (1 : 2).

questions.q: 10.0 mL of Na<sub>2</sub>CO<sub>3</sub> solution is titrated against 0.2 M HCl solution. The following titre values were obtained in 5 readings: 4.8 mL, 4.9 mL, 5.0 mL, 5.0 mL and 5.0 mL. Based on these readings, and convention of titrimetric estimation the concentration of Na<sub>2</sub>CO<sub>3</sub> solution is ____ mM. (Round off to the Nearest integer)
questions.sol:
Concordant titre = 5.0 mL. Na₂CO₃ + 2HCl → 2NaCl + H₂O + CO₂.

HCl = 0.2 × 5.0 = 1.0 mmol → Na₂CO₃ = 0.5 mmol in 10.0 mL → 0.05 M = 50 mM.
questions.hint: Use the repeated (concordant) reading and the 1 : 2 ratio.

questions.q: The volume of HCl, containing 73 g L<sup>−1</sup>, required to completely neutralise NaOH obtained by reacting 0.69 g of metallic sodium with water, is ____ mL. (Nearest Integer) (Given: molar masses of Na, Cl, O, H are 23, 35.5, 16 and 1 g mol<sup>−1</sup> respectively)
questions.sol:
0.69 g Na = 0.03 mol → 0.03 mol NaOH → needs 0.03 mol HCl.

HCl solution: 73 g L⁻¹ ÷ 36.5 = 2 M. Volume = 0.03 ÷ 2 = 0.015 L = 15 mL.
questions.hint: g L⁻¹ ÷ molar mass = molarity.

questions.q: 100 g of propane is completely reacted with 1000 g of oxygen. The mole fraction of carbon dioxide in the resulting mixture is x × 10<sup>−2</sup>. The value of x is ____. (Nearest integer) [Atomic weight: H = 1.008; C = 12.00; O = 16.00]
questions.sol:
C₃H₈ + 5O₂ → 3CO₂ + 4H₂O. Propane = 100 ÷ 44.06 = 2.27 mol; O₂ = 31.25 mol (needs only 11.35), so propane is limiting.

Final: CO₂ 6.81 mol, H₂O 9.08 mol, O₂ left 19.90 mol (total 35.79 mol).

x(CO₂) = 6.81 ÷ 35.79 = 0.19 → 19.

NTA's answer counts the water in the mixture. If water is taken as liquid and left out, x(CO₂) would be 0.25.
questions.hint: Find the limiting reagent, then list every species left at the end.

questions.q: 1 gram of sodium hydroxide was treated with 25 mL of 0.75 M HCl solution, the mass of sodium hydroxide left unreacted is equal to
questions.sol:
NaOH = 1/40 = 0.025 mol. HCl = 0.025 L × 0.75 M = 0.01875 mol.

NaOH + HCl → NaCl + H₂O (1 : 1), so HCl is the limiting reagent.

NaOH left = 0.025 − 0.01875 = 0.00625 mol × 40 = 0.25 g = 250 mg.
questions.hint: Moles of HCl = molarity × volume in litres; compare with moles of NaOH.

questions.q: 250 mL of 0.5 M NaOH was added to 500 mL of 1 M HCl. The number of unreacted HCl molecules in the solution after complete reaction is ____ × 10<sup>21</sup>. (Nearest integer) (N<sub>A</sub> = 6.022 × 10<sup>23</sup>)
questions.sol:
NaOH = 0.125 mol, HCl = 0.500 mol (1 : 1). NaOH is limiting.

HCl left = 0.375 mol × 6.022 × 10²³ = 2.258 × 10²³ = 226 × 10²¹.
questions.hint: Moles = M × V(L) for each; subtract.

questions.q: 2 L of 0.2 M H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> is reacted with 2 L of 0.1 M NaOH solution, the molarity of the resulting product Na<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> in the solution is ____ millimolar. (Nearest integer)
questions.sol:
H₂SO₄ = 0.4 mol, NaOH = 0.2 mol. H₂SO₄ + 2NaOH → Na₂SO₄ + 2H₂O, so NaOH is limiting and gives 0.1 mol Na₂SO₄.

Total volume 4 L → 0.025 M = 25 mM.
questions.hint: Find the limiting reagent, then divide by the combined volume.

questions.q: The mole fraction of glucose (C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>12</sub>O<sub>6</sub>) in an aqueous binary solution is 0.1. The mass percentage of water in it, to the nearest integer, is ____.
questions.sol:
Take 1 mol in total: 0.1 mol glucose (18 g) and 0.9 mol water (16.2 g).

Mass % of water = 16.2 ÷ 34.2 × 100 = 47.4 ≈ 47.
questions.hint: Pick 1 mol total and turn the moles into grams.

questions.check: Worked out independently (the source copy prints no answer key)
questions.q: At T(K), 100 g of 98% H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> (w/w) aqueous solution is mixed with 100 g of 49% H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> (w/w) aqueous solution. What is the mole fraction of H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> in the resultant solution? (Given: Atomic mass H = 1u; S = 32u; O = 16u). (Assume that temperature after mixing remains constant)
questions.hint: Add up acid and water separately before converting to moles.

questions.check: Worked out independently (the source copy prints no answer key)
questions.q: What is the mole fraction of water in 10% by weight (w/w) of aqueous urea solution? [Given: Molar mass of H, O, C and N are 1, 16, 12 and 14 g mol<sup>−1</sup> respectively.]
questions.sol:
100 g solution: urea 10 g = 0.167 mol; water 90 g = 5 mol.

x(water) = 5 ÷ 5.167 = 0.967.
questions.hint: Take 100 g; urea's molar mass is 60.

questions.check: Worked out independently (the source copy prints no answer key)
questions.q:
Given below are two statements: Given: Molar mass of C, H, O, Cl are 12, 1, 16 and 35.5 g mol−1, respectively.
Statement I: In 30% (w/w) solution of methanol in CCl4 (at T K), the mole fraction of CCl4 is equal to 0.33.
Statement II: Mixture of methanol and CCl4 shows positive deviation from Raoult's law.
In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:
o: Both Statement I and Statement II are true
Both Statement I and Statement II are false
Statement I is true but Statement II is false
Statement I is false but Statement II is true
questions.sol:
100 g: methanol 30 g = 0.9375 mol, CCl₄ 70 g = 0.4545 mol → x(CCl₄) = 0.4545 ÷ 1.392 = 0.33 ✓.

Methanol's hydrogen bonds are broken on mixing with CCl₄, so the mixture shows positive deviation ✓ (Class 12, Solutions). Both true.
questions.hint: Statement I is a mass% → mole fraction conversion.

questions.q: Given a solution of HNO<sub>3</sub> of density 1.4 g/mL and 63% w/w. Determine molarity of HNO<sub>3</sub> solution.
questions.sol:
Take 100 g of solution: 63 g HNO₃ = 63/63 = 1 mol.

Volume of 100 g solution = 100 ÷ 1.4 = 71.4 mL = 0.0714 L.

Molarity = 1 ÷ 0.0714 = 14 M. (Shortcut: M = 10 × d × w% ÷ molar mass = 10 × 1.4 × 63 ÷ 63 = 14.)
questions.hint: Assume 100 g of solution; use density to get its volume.

questions.q: A commercially sold conc. HCl is 35% HCl by mass. If the density of this commercial acid is 1.46 g/mL, the molarity of this solution is: (Atomic mass: Cl = 35.5 amu, H = 1 amu)
questions.sol:
1 L of acid weighs 1460 g, of which 35% = 511 g is HCl = 511 ÷ 36.5 = 14.0 mol.

Molarity = 14.0 M.
questions.hint: Mass of 1 L from density, then take 35% of it.

questions.q: Calculate the molarity of a solution having density = 1.5 g/mL, %(w/w) of solute is 36% and molecular weight of solute is 36 g/mol.
questions.sol:
100 g solution: 36 g solute = 1 mol; volume = 100 ÷ 1.5 = 66.7 mL.

Molarity = 1 ÷ 0.0667 = 15 M.
questions.hint: M = 10 × d × w% ÷ molar mass.

questions.q: 70% by mass solution of HNO<sub>3</sub> is taken having density 1.41 g/mL. Calculate the molarity of solution (nearest integer).
questions.hint: 100 g solution → 70 g HNO₃; volume = 100 ÷ 1.41 mL.

questions.q: A solution of two components containing n<sub>1</sub> moles of the 1st component and n<sub>2</sub> moles of the 2nd component is prepared. M<sub>1</sub> and M<sub>2</sub> are the molecular weights of component 1 and 2 respectively. If d is the density of the solution in g mL<sup>−1</sup>, C<sub>2</sub> is the molarity and x<sub>2</sub> is the mole fraction of the 2nd component, then C<sub>2</sub> can be expressed as:
questions.sol:
Take 1 mol of solution in total: x₂ mol of component 2 and x₁ = 1 − x₂ mol of component 1.

Mass = x₁M₁ + x₂M₂ = M₁ + x₂(M₂ − M₁) g, so volume = [M₁ + x₂(M₂ − M₁)] ÷ d mL.

C₂ = x₂ ÷ (volume in L) = 1000 d x₂ / [M₁ + x₂(M₂ − M₁)].
questions.hint: Choose 1 mol of solution; find its mass, then its volume from d.

questions.also: Statements C and D come from Class 12 Unit 1 (Solutions, Henry's law).
questions.q:
Identify the correct statements:
(A) The molality of 2.5 g of ethanoic acid (Molar mass: 60 g mol−1) in 75 g of benzene solution is 0.556 m.
(B) The molarity of a solution containing 5 g of NaOH (molar mass: 40 g mol−1) in 450 mL of solution is 0.278 M at 298 K.
(C) Aquatic species are more comfortable in cold water.
(D) The solubility of gas increases with decrease in pressure.
(E) For a binary mixture of A and B, the number of moles of A and B are nA and nB respectively. The mole fraction of B will be xB = nA/(nA + nB).
questions.sol:
• A ✓ 2.5/60 = 0.0417 mol ÷ 0.075 kg = 0.556 m
  • B ✓ 5/40 = 0.125 mol ÷ 0.450 L = 0.278 M
  • C ✓ Gases dissolve better at lower temperature, so cold water holds more O₂
  • D ✗ Gas solubility increases with pressure (Henry's law)
  • E ✗ xB = nB/(nA + nB); the numerator must be B's moles
questions.hint: Check A and B numerically; E is a definition check.

questions.q: The mole fraction of a solute in a 100 molal aqueous solution is ____ × 10<sup>−2</sup>. (Round off to the Nearest Integer) [Given: Atomic masses: H: 1.0 u, O: 16.0 u]
questions.sol:
100 molal: 100 mol solute in 1000 g water = 55.56 mol water.

x(solute) = 100 ÷ (100 + 55.56) = 0.643 = 64 × 10⁻².
questions.hint: Molality fixes moles of solute per 1000 g of water.

questions.q: A 6.50 molal solution of KOH (aq.) has a density of 1.89 g cm<sup>−3</sup>. The molarity of the solution is ____ mol dm<sup>−3</sup>. (Round off to the Nearest Integer) [Atomic masses: K: 39.0 u; O: 16.0 u; H: 1.0 u]
questions.sol:
1000 g water holds 6.50 mol KOH = 6.50 × 56 = 364 g. Solution mass = 1364 g → volume = 1364 ÷ 1.89 = 721.7 mL.

Molarity = 6.50 ÷ 0.7217 = 9.0 ≈ 9.
questions.hint: Start from 1 kg of solvent (molality), add solute mass, divide by density.

questions.q: An aqueous KCl solution of density 1.20 g mL<sup>−1</sup> has a molality of 3.30 mol kg<sup>−1</sup>. The molarity of the solution in mol L<sup>−1</sup> is ____ (Nearest integer) [Molar mass of KCl = 74.5]
questions.hint: Molality → 1 kg solvent; add solute; volume from density.

questions.q: What is the mass ratio of ethylene glycol (C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>6</sub>O<sub>2</sub>, molar mass = 62 g/mol) required for making 500 g of 0.25 molal aqueous solution and 250 mL of 0.25 molar aqueous solution?
questions.hint: 500 g is the solution mass (solvent + solute), not the solvent.

questions.q: The density of 3 M solution of NaCl is 1.0 g mL<sup>−1</sup>. Molality of the solution is ____ × 10<sup>−2</sup> m. (Nearest integer). Given: Molar mass of Na and Cl is 23 and 35.5 g mol<sup>−1</sup> respectively.
